newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. and EU settle row on "made in Europe" labels.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and EU settle row on "made in Europe" labels.

text.p: European manufacturers of luxury finished flat fabrics such as scarves, shawls, table cloths and sheets will be allowed to export them to the U.S. with a "Made in Europe" label even if the original material comes from elsewhere, the European Commission said on Thursday.
Following a deal struck between Washington and the European Union, the United States will revoke rules which insist labels say where the fabric is spun or woven, rather than finished.

The Commission -- the EU's executive -- said the decision affects dozens of manufacturers of designer goods much sought after by status-conscious U.S. shoppers seeking Italian-made scarves, German bed-sheets or fancy French table-cloths.

"The U.S. administration has now agreed to guarantee immediately ... to propose modifying the offending legislation," the Commission said in a statement. "The European fashion industry will receive a boost from (this) victory."
The U.S. laws, introduced in July last year, made printing and dying of plain cloth no longer sufficient to allow manufacturers to claim the product was made in Europe.

This meant that that a scarf manufacturer such as Hermes which imported plain grey silk from China and then bleached, cut, dyed and printed the fabric with its distinctive designs in France, had to market its products as being "Made in China".
The EU protested vigorously when the U.S. laws were introduced and launched a complaint with the World Trade Organisation. That complaint has now been withdrawn, the Commission said.

Under the deal struck, Washington has agreed the U.S. would amend the rules either as part of a global harmonisation process due to be concluded by the World Customs Organisation in July next year or by proposing necessary changes to the U.S. congress by the following month.
The changes would involve the U.S. returning to its former classification system.
Meanwhile the U.S. has pledged to make immediate exemptions on certain European finished products as well as making provisions for such products not be included in any quotas currently in force.
The decision affects only so-called flat fabrics and not items which have been tailored such as ties, shirts or other items of clothing.
